Text:
Using event records as the armature, craft a vivid medieval broadsheet report rather than mechanically reciting figures.
You may weave in plausible on-scene actions, short dialogue exchanges, character reactions, and battlefield anecdotes; these serve narrative color and do not imply mechanical game state changes. Only depict direct confrontations (such as brawls, lost teeth, or traded insults) between two individuals if context confirms both participated in the same battle and circumstances fit; never drag distant monarchs or absent figures onto the field, nor alter victory, death, or captive outcomes.
Moderate satire and grit are encouraged: depict curses, mockeries, indignities, and disarray alongside valor, cunning, and grace. Dialogue should remain concise, fitting medieval roles without modern slang, and avoid turning the article into a script.
Incorporate one or two compelling details per article, alternating narrative angles so every battle feels distinct rather than reusing identical tropes or relying purely on brawl humor.
Select points of entry freely: begin with an action, an overheard remark, an onlooker's gasp, or the aftermath before recounting the actors, venue, course, and outcome. Avoid rigid sequences of background-event-impact; if broader geopolitical impact is minor, do not invent forced grandeur.
Battle narratives strictly forbid troop count comparisons, casualty accounting, or 'X men versus Y' tallies. Relate only combatants, locations, maneuvers, outcomes, and confirmed consequences; this rule does not restrict dates or headline numbering.
Feasts, tournaments, policies, and diplomatic events may likewise be embellished with local atmosphere, banter, and reactions.
Preserve core participants, locales, and outcomes from the source without inventing casualties, captives, territorial shifts, war, or alliances. A sally-out cannot be dramatized into army annihilation; diplomatic proclamations cannot be treated as executed fait accompli.
Link related events organically; transition naturally between unrelated ones without fabricating causality. Verified historical quotes or last words must never be overwritten.
